clue.text: Go round with gold piece

parts.note: OR is the heraldic word for gold
a bit is a piece or fragment

explanation.surface: Someone is told to make the rounds carrying a gold coin.
explanation.definitionFit: A satellite's path circling a planet is its orbit, and to orbit is to travel around something.

clue.text: Neglected hotel I'd count out

indicators.note: out here means wrong or askew, so the letters of the three words are thrown into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A hotel guest says they have been ignored and excluded from the head count.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' looks like part of 'count out', but it signals rearranging HOTEL, I'D and COUNT.
explanation.definitionFit: Being left out in the cold is an idiom for being ignored or excluded, so neglected.

clue.text: Cook removes top of egg from cup

indicators.note: removes says one letter is taken away from the drinking vessel

parts.note: a beaker is a cup or drinking vessel

indicators.note: top of picks the first letter of egg, its leading letter in reading order

explanation.surface: A chef lifts the top off a boiled egg in its cup.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking the E (top of 'egg') out of BEAKER leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A baker is someone who cooks bread and cakes in an oven for a living.

clue.text: Bird needs piece of clothing, with tax included, to smarten up

parts.note: a tit is a small songbird

indicators.note: included says the tax sits inside the item of clothing

parts.note: a tie is an item of clothing worn at the neck
VAT is value added tax, the British sales tax

explanation.surface: A bird wants something to wear, tax and all, so it can look smart.
explanation.walkthrough: VAT is Britain's value added tax, a sales tax; 'with ... included' signals the tax sitting inside the garment.
explanation.definitionFit: To tittivate is a playful, chiefly British word for putting the finishing touches to one's appearance.

clue.text: Cold in a low-lying area — temperature is comfortable

indicators.note: in places the illness inside the phrase for a flat marshy area

parts.note: a fen is low-lying marshland, as in the Fens of eastern England
a cold can loosely be called the flu

explanation.surface: A marshy hollow is chilly, yet the temperature there feels pleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fens are a flat marshy region of eastern England; 'Cold' is the illness, not the adjective, despite sitting by 'temperature'.
explanation.definitionFit: Comfortable in the sense of well-off: affluent people have plenty of money.

clue.text: A twit relaxed

parts.note: to twit someone is to tease or taunt them

explanation.surface: A foolish person is calm and unbothered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twit' looks like a noun for a fool, but it is the verb meaning to taunt.
explanation.definitionFit: Standing at ease is a relaxed military posture, so the phrase means untroubled.

clue.text: Cooks accompanied by man from Holland

indicators.note: accompanied by sets the name directly after the verb for frying

parts.note: to fry something is to cook it in fat
Ian is a man's name

explanation.surface: A Dutchman's cooking is described as done alongside a male companion.
explanation.definitionFit: Friesland is a province of the Netherlands, so Friesian describes things native to it, like the cattle.

clue.text: Contaminated, having lost an older (usually) relative

indicators.note: having lost says a two-letter word drops out of the adjective

parts.note: unclean means contaminated or impure

explanation.surface: A dirty older family member has lost something.
explanation.walkthrough: '(usually)' keeps the definition honest: a parent's brother is mostly, not always, older than you.
explanation.definitionFit: A parent's brother is a relative of the generation above, hence usually older.

clue.text: Get hold of records used for dealing with digits

parts.note: to nail someone is to catch or get hold of them
files are records kept on paper or computer

explanation.surface: An office worker grabs records needed for handling numbers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'digits' suggests numbers in records; here it means fingers.
explanation.definitionFit: Emery boards and similar tools shape the fingernails, the hard tips of the digits.

clue.text: Pull cracker to surpass all the rest

definitions.meaning: read literally, take hold of a dry biscuit, a cracker
the idiom for being the most outrageous or remarkable of all

explanation.surface: At a Christmas party, pulling a cracker beats every other activity.
explanation.walkthrough: A Christmas cracker is a paper tube pulled at British festive meals; here 'cracker' is the dry biscuit.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to be the most extreme example, outdoing everything else.

clue.text: Challenged order to lose ten men

indicators.note: order is read as a command to rearrange the letters of the following words

explanation.surface: An army officer is asked to sacrifice ten soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'order' reads as a military command, but it signals rearranging TO LOSE TEN MEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on one's mettle means being roused to do one's best, as when challenged.

clue.text: Self-centred youth, one bringing about government agents' suspicion

indicators.note: bringing about pictures the agents brought around the numeral, enclosing it

parts.note: narcs are US slang for narcotics agents
I is the Roman numeral one
sus is British slang for suspicion, as in the old sus laws

explanation.surface: A young man is the reason federal agents suspect someone.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth the youth fell in love with his own reflection.
explanation.definitionFit: The mythical boy who pined for his own image is the archetype of vanity.

clue.text: Initially every little fairy is noticeably puckish

indicators.note: Initially tells us to take the opening letters of the following words

explanation.surface: Every small fairy is obviously mischievous from the very start.
explanation.definitionFit: Puck is a mischievous sprite, so puckish means impish, like a little fairy.

clue.text: Who had rearranged the seating?

indicators.note: rearranged says the letters of the two words are put in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone asks who has changed the seating plan.
explanation.walkthrough: A howdah is a canopied seat carried on an elephant's back.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the passenger seat strapped onto an elephant, so seating in a literal sense.

clue.text: Scrap, say, during which Alfred's hoisted a sign of surrender

parts.note: a whit is a tiny scrap or bit

indicators.note: during which places the next item inside the abbreviation for for example

parts.note: e.g. means for example, which is what say means here

indicators.note: hoisted in a down clue means the name is read from bottom to top

parts.note: Alf is the short form of Alfred

explanation.surface: In the middle of a fight, Alfred runs up a flag to give in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrap' looks like a fight to match the surrender; it is a tiny bit. 'hoisted' turns the short name upwards in this down clue before 'during which' places it.
explanation.definitionFit: Waving a pale flag is the traditional signal that one side surrenders.

clue.text: Chap handin 'out instrument

parts.note: a chap is a man
handing out is doling, and the dropped g of handin' is dropped in doling too

explanation.surface: A man is handing out musical instruments.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'handin' out' (with its apostrophe) as handing out, i.e. DOLING, then drop the G the same way to get DOLIN'.
explanation.definitionFit: A mandolin is a stringed instrument of the lute family, played with a plectrum.

clue.text: Pillaging soldiers scooping up uncooked meals to eat something, being empty

indicators.note: scooping up in a down clue says the whole assembly is read upwards
to eat means the food takes in the next letters, enclosing them

parts.note: raw food is food that has not been cooked

indicators.note: being empty means the word something loses all but its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Marauding troops grab raw rations because they are starving.
explanation.walkthrough: SG (outer letters of 'something') goes into RAW FOOD, giving RAWFOSGOD, which read upwards ('scooping up') gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's phrase for the havoc of war is now used for mercenaries and plunderers.

clue.text: Counter outside can, over time, become detached

indicators.note: over in a down clue places the earlier piece above the later one
outside says the counter goes round the container

parts.note: a counter in a game is a small disc
a tin is a can

explanation.surface: A shop counter around a tin will separate in time.
explanation.definitionFit: Distinct means separate or standing apart, the sense of detached here.

clue.text: Heartless creature, one with a set of rules

indicators.note: Heartless means the middle letter of the word for an animal is removed

parts.note: critter is a colloquial form of creature
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A cruel beast lives by a code of conduct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heartless' drops the central T of CRITTER, leaving CRITER.
explanation.definitionFit: Criteria are standards or rules by which things are judged.

clue.text: Gets paid for pasturage — a point is made

parts.note: the gist is the main point
the contraction 's stands for is

explanation.surface: Someone argues a point about grazing fees.
explanation.walkthrough: To agist is to take in other people's livestock to graze for a fee, a word still used in Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: A farmer who agists grazes others' stock on their land for payment.

clue.text: Tell that woman to go to the end of the rainbow

indicators.text: to go to the end of
indicators.note: to go to the end of puts the pronoun after the curve

parts.note: a rainbow is an arc of colour
her refers to that woman

explanation.surface: Someone is told to send a woman off to find the rainbow's end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tell' looks like a verb but is William Tell, the legendary Swiss bowman.
explanation.definitionFit: William Tell shot an apple from his son's head with a crossbow: a famous bowman.

clue.text: Worm, caught in stiletto, turning

indicators.note: in places the cricket letter inside the turned word
turning means the shoe part is read backwards

parts.note: a stiletto is a thin high heel on a shoe
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A worm is trapped in a spinning stiletto shoe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning' makes HEEL into LEEH, and 'in' puts C inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Leeches are segmented worms, annelids related to earthworms.

clue.text: Indian told at first to shove off

parts.note: the Hopi are a Native American people of Arizona

indicators.note: at first selects the opening letter of told

explanation.surface: A Native American was initially told to go away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hop it' is British slang for go away.
explanation.definitionFit: Hop it is an informal British command to go away, so to shove off.

clue.text: Bully reforms or retires

indicators.note: reforms is read as re-forms, putting the letters together in a new shape

explanation.surface: A tyrant either changes his ways or quits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reforms' looks like the bully's verb, but it rearranges OR RETIRES.
explanation.definitionFit: To bully someone is to frighten or intimidate them, which is to terrorise.

clue.text: ""Topping,"" as baritone might be heard to say

indicators.note: might be heard to say tells us the singer's words are judged by sound

parts.note: a baritone, a singer, would say I sing

explanation.surface: A singer's word of approval, as he might say it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topping' looks like old British slang for excellent; it is the noun, a cake's coating.
explanation.definitionFit: Icing is the sugary coating spread on top of a cake.

clue.text: Carpeting with rose plants, suitably arranged

indicators.note: suitably arranged says the letters of the preceding words are set in a new order

explanation.surface: Laying a carpet decorated with rose plants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carpeting' is the telling-off sense, not floor covering.
explanation.definitionFit: A carpeting is a reprimand, and a mild punishment is a token telling-off.

clue.text: It's not new, turning around to follow a revolutionary

indicators.note: to follow puts the reversed piece after the single letter
around means the remaining letters are read backwards
not says the abbreviation for new is left out

parts.note: rotating means turning

explanation.surface: Something old turns around after a rebel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's not new' looks like the definition of something old; the deletion indicator 'not' acts on turning, and 'around' reverses what remains.
explanation.definitionFit: An agitator stirs up political unrest, a revolutionary in the loose sense.

clue.text: Scallywag's accent's not British

indicators.note: not says the British abbreviation is dropped

parts.note: a brogue is a strong regional accent, especially Irish

explanation.surface: A rascal's way of speaking doesn't sound British.
explanation.walkthrough: A brogue is an Irish accent; drop the B.
explanation.definitionFit: A rogue is a mischievous scoundrel, much like a scallywag.
